title: Delhi Teen Aadvik Jain Wins Diana Award for Menstrual Health Work
excerpt: The 18-year-old founder of Team Period is among 198 young people from 44 countries honoured in 2026, after building a school campaign on workshops, surveys and pad access.
body:
• Aadvik Jain, 18, of Delhi is among 198 young people from 44 countries named as 2026 Diana Award recipients, announced on November 4.
  • He leads Team Period, founded in 2024 with three school friends to challenge menstrual stigma through workshops, performances and campaigns.
  • The Diana Award's official Roll of Honour says his work has reached more than 5,000 people, and Team Period has installed a sanitary pad dispenser at his school.
  • Jain is set to start studying medicine and public health at the University of Bologna in Italy in February.

Aadvik Jain, an 18-year-old student from Delhi, has been named a recipient of the 2026 Diana Award for leading Team Period, a youth initiative working to end shame and stigma around menstruation in India. He is one of 198 young people from 44 countries honoured this year, announced on November 4 at a virtual ceremony, according to NPR.

The Diana Award, established in memory of Diana, Princess of Wales, recognises young people aged 16 to 25 for social action and humanitarian work. India accounted for nearly a quarter of this year's recipients, with 49 honorees, NPR reported.

It started with a friend's struggle

Jain told NPR the work began in 2023, when he was in the tenth grade and noticed a close friend struggling during midterm examinations. She told him she was on her period and having really bad cramps, and she was taken to the school medical room, given a painkiller and sent home with her parents. She had been experiencing severe cramps for six to eight months, Jain said, and her periods before that had been very irregular, but her parents initially thought she was trying to get out of her examinations.

After Jain spoke to his mother, she spoke to a teacher, who contacted the friend's parents and encouraged them to see a doctor. She was diagnosed with PCOS, now referred to as PMOS, and doctors were also investigating endometriosis, according to NPR. She received treatment and gradually improved — an experience Jain, who became concerned about menstrual health at 14, said stayed with him.

"What if a girl could simply tell her father, 'Dad, I'm having really bad cramps, and I can't go to school today,' and he would say, 'Okay, let me get you a heating pad'?"

Jain contrasted that with an injury of his own, when his father left an office two hours away to take him to an emergency room after he broke his little toe — menstrual pain, in his telling, should draw the same concern.

From a school competition to Team Period

Jain studied at Amity International School, which runs a programme called Youth Power through its student newspaper, The Global Times, in which teams of four students choose a social cause and work for several months to create change. His team was himself, Shivansh Arora, Aaratrika Jha Anand and Navya Manglik — two boys and two girls.

Team Period was started in 2024, and what began as a school competition entry continued after the competition ended. The NPR interview published by WESA describes the group challenging menstrual stigma through workshops, street performances, awareness campaigns and efforts to improve access to menstrual pads and products.

The Diana Award's official citation adds scale: Jain has led Team Period since 2024 with a mission to "Unshackle the Shame and Unleash the Power," through social media campaigns, podcasts, flashmobs, workshops and health camps. His work has reached more than 5,000 people, the citation says, "from young girls living in slums to menopausal women in gated communities."

Surveys, performances and a pad dispenser

Jain said Team Period has collected around 4,000 survey responses from students, parents and the wider community. The team installed a sanitary pad dispenser at its school, and Jain said they are talking to companies about making dispensers available to other schools at a nominal cost. The Diana Award citation also points to distribution drives in underserved communities.

The group has also used performance to open conversations. Jain described a dance drama set during Durga Puja, performed before an audience of more than 500 people in April 2025, and a flash mob at a mall. In workshops, after boys were asked to leave one session so girls could speak freely, Jain said they later held a separate session for the boys and eventually brought everyone together.

Jain told NPR the work has largely been concentrated in Delhi — in government schools, orphanages, underserved neighbourhoods and his own school — and that the team now wants to create local chapters as members spread out for their studies.

What the award does — and does not — provide

Jain was explicit that the Diana Award does not come with prize money. What it gives, he said, is recognition that the work matters, credibility with potential sponsors and partners, and a platform to take the work to a larger audience.

Next, Jain is set to start studying medicine and public health at the University of Bologna in Italy in February, according to NPR. He said he hopes one day to work with an organisation like the World Health Organization or the United Nations. For diaspora readers, his path — from a Delhi classroom to an Italian university — is the next chapter of a campaign that began at 14 with a question about why a friend's pain was not being taken seriously.
